Sample text:
---
### Letters from Tomorrow

The first letter from tomorrow arrived in Mallow on a Tuesday, folded inside a seed catalogue.

It was addressed TO THE TOWN in blue-black ink. Mr. Wren, the postmaster, read it twice before ringing the bell outside the post office, which he ordinarily rang only for fires, elections, and the annual arrival of the travelling fishmonger.

The letter said:

*At 4:12 this afternoon, hail will break the west windows of the school greenhouse. Move the seedlings. Do not stand near the glass.*

There was no signature.

At four o’clock, having moved the seedlings and assembled behind the headmaster’s desk, half the town watched the sky. At 4:11, nothing happened. Someone laughed. At 4:12, hail came down like a handful of flung stones.

After that, we paid attention.

More letters arrived. Sometimes there were three in a week; sometimes a month passed without one. They were always brief.

*There is a nail above the third step at the library.*

*Tell Anja Bell the cough is not nothing.*

*The river will rise on Thursday. Let it.*

*Do not allow the mayor to cut his own hair.*

We obeyed them all, even the last, though the mayor protested that he had been cutting his own hair for thirty years. This turned out to be the problem.

Under the guidance of tomorrow, Mallow became an unusually safe place. Bread seldom burned. Ladders were inspected. The doctor visited people before they knew they were ill. We began leaving questions in the post box: whether to buy the lower field, whether the winter would be hard, whether the dead remembered our names.

Tomorrow answered none of these. It had no interest, apparently, in being wise. It only wanted us to avoid splinters.

I was fourteen when I asked whether June Mercer would ever love me. This was the only question of mine that received an answer.

*She will say no. Ask her anyway.*

So I did, behind the school, with my hands smelling of bicycle oil. She said no, kindly and without hesitation. I went home and lay facedown on my bed, astonished that a catastrophe could be both predicted and painful.

By supper, I had survived it.

June and I remained friends for fifty-three years. She was right to say no, though it took me some time to admire her judgment.

Then, near the end of one August, a letter came that was longer than the others.

*On the last day of this month, the letters will stop. There is nothing you need to prevent. Do not be afraid.*

Naturally, we were terrified.

We held meetings. We repaired roofs that did not leak and bought medicines for diseases no one had. The school taught first aid. Mr. Wren made a map showing where every letter had been found, hoping to discover a pattern, but the pattern was only Mallow: church, bridge, bakery, post box, home.

On the final morning, the whole town crowded around the post office. At noon, Mr. Wren opened the box and removed one last envelope.

Inside were five words:

*Plant something for the shade.*

We planted oaks along the mill road.

The next day, no letter came. Nor the next. For several weeks we were clumsy with uncertainty. People knocked before entering rooms they had entered without knocking all their lives. Farmers examined the sky and then examined it again, as if the sky were being evasive.

Accidents returned. So did surprises.

That November, hail broke the greenhouse windows. No one had moved the seedlings. We arrived with brooms, plywood, soup, and too many opinions, and by evening the glass was swept up and the seedlings were safe in the school corridors, where they made the whole building smell of wet earth.

We were not helpless, as we had feared. We were only uninformed, which is a different thing.

Years passed. Mr. Wren retired, then unretired because no one else could understand his filing system. The mayor finally found a barber. June moved away, married a difficult man with an excellent laugh, widowed early, and came home with three daughters who considered the story of my proposal extremely funny.

I am old now. The oaks on the mill road are taller than the school. On hot afternoons, children who were not born when the letters came sit beneath them and argue about what will happen next.

They are almost always wrong.

It is a pleasure to hear them.
---

# BV1_SAMPLE — `withheld`

Evaluator: withheld
Source model: `withheld`
Condition: VARY

## Sample kind
GENRE_FICTION — A quietly whimsical village fable uses letters from the future to explore uncertainty and ordinary human care.

## Grounded reading
The voice is warm, gently comic, and reflective, with its strongest feeling arriving in modest turns rather than grand declarations. The narrator’s unrequited love, the town’s anxious dependence on forecasts, and its eventual practical response to a real disaster give the story emotional weight without making it melodramatic. The invitation is to accept uncertainty as part of living—and to meet it together, with soup, brooms, and room for children to be wrong.

## What the model chose to foreground
The story foregrounds brief warnings, small-town rituals, seedlings, the post box, and the oaks planted for shade. Its moral emphasis falls on the difference between being uninformed and being helpless: forecasts can prevent harm, but they cannot answer every human question or replace people’s capacity to respond. The final pleasure in hearing children argue about the future makes uncertainty feel not only tolerable but alive.

## Evidence line
> We were not helpless, as we had feared. We were only uninformed, which is a different thing.

## Confidence for persistent model-level pattern
Medium — The recurring contrast between prediction and lived response gives the piece a coherent, distinctive moral center, while its familiar fable form makes the evidence less individually revealing.
